hits.name: elvis
hits.text:
Learn to build a custom harness, folks.

This Microsoft work builds a harness to improve long-context reasoning without synthetic data or post-training.

(bookmark it)

They show that Llama3-8B gains 64.18 points on average across long-context benchmarks with no training at all. The gain comes from the harness.

It breaks long-context tasks into capability primitives. A strong agent then rewrites those primitives, the state they track, and the control logic over many rounds of self-improvement on a development set.

The harness built for Llama3-8B transfers to Qwen2.5-3B. On HELMET and RULER, it beats NExtLong and PolicyLong, which rely on data synthesis and training, at less than half their estimated cost.

The harness is written by GPT-5.6-Sol, and results drop sharply when the small models build their own.

The takeaway: before post-training a small model for long context, try improving the harness around it.

https://t.co/DL74eulFOR

hits.name: Akshay 🚀
hits.text:
Your agent remembers too much.

Decision models like Jev can fix that.

Let me explain:

A common agent-memory pipeline sends conversations, tool results, and task outcomes to an extractor.

The extractor proposes possible memories, including user preferences, facts, and procedures.

Take a travel assistant, and look at what the user says:

- I usually prefer an aisle seat.
- For this flight, book a window seat.
- The flight is delayed by 25 minutes.

These statements should not be stored in the same way.

The aisle-seat preference can help with later bookings. The window-seat request belongs to a single flight.

The delay has no use once the flight is over.

A strong memory system may already make this kind of distinction.

It can record where a fact came from and resolve it against facts already stored. It can also track when a fact becomes valid or invalid.

If the source has enough context, the window-seat request can stay tied to one trip.

So you should not add a decision model just to repeat what the memory system already does.

A decision model becomes useful when the app has its own rules for what may enter long-term memory.

A travel app might require that:

- Only preferences the user stated or confirmed become account-level memories.
- A preference inferred from one booking stays attached to that trip.
- Passport numbers and payment details never go into general memory.
- Ambiguous candidates stay in the session until the user confirms them.

These rules need semantic judgment. Once a candidate is classified, ordinary code can enforce the policy.

The hard part is telling a lasting preference from a one-time instruction, or from weak evidence for an inferred preference.

A decision model can make that decision before the app writes anything to long-term memory.

For each candidate, the app sends the decision model the proposed fact and its source evidence. It also sends the current user, trip, and session state.

It can ask typed questions like these:

- Did the user state the preference in explicit terms?
- Should it apply past the current trip?
- What retention scope should it have?
- Would reuse on a later booking create a real risk?

The decision model returns choices, scores, and probabilities. Several questions can share the same state in a single request.

Application code then applies the thresholds:

↳ Store the aisle-seat preference for the user.
↳ Keep the window-seat request attached to this trip.
↳ Leave the delay in the current session.
↳ Reject sensitive fields before they enter general memory.

The app can then send approved candidates as episodes to a memory system such as Graphiti. Graphiti runs extraction, entity resolution, provenance, temporal updates, and retrieval.

Graphiti is open source if you want to inspect that memory layer:
https://t.co/uR6rXYx05Y

If Graphiti's current ingestion already meets the needs of your app, a decision model is unnecessary.

Add a decision model when you need to check product-specific rules before anything is sent to Graphiti. That includes whether a preference was confirmed, and whether a fact is safe to store.

If decision models are new to you, I explained how Jev works in the article quoted below.

Great paper from Meta with practical tips for tuning LLM judges.

This one is on keeping LLM code judges calibrated and tested on a deployed coding agent.

LLM judges often decide whether an agent's code change is good. But their prompts go stale every time the agent changes.

AutoRefine fixes the prompt using signals teams already have, like whether tests passed and whether the change got merged.

On Meta's deployed agent, agreement between the judge and real outcomes rose from 0.16 to 0.51.

https://t.co/dYYYr0uxRq

hits.text:
I'm bullish on new architectures for long-running agents.

But long context needs to be practical to serve.

Sugar Glider is a new family of LLM architectures from @i14labs built for long contexts.

It keeps a fixed-size KV cache as context grows. At one million tokens, i14 reports up to 32x more requests per server than its baseline model.

What does this mean in practice?

Your agents could keep much longer histories without constantly trimming or summarizing them.

And you can choose that memory size at deployment without retraining.

hits.name: elvis
hits.text:
Impressive paper from Robbyant on physical AI.

(bookmark it)

Robot hands use a range of tactile sensors, and a model trained on one sensor can struggle to transfer to another.

That's a big challenge in robotics right now.

LingBot-Touch is a foundation model to address this challenge. It was pretrained on 4,983 hours of real touch data.

They tested it on the XHand1, a robot hand whose sensor the model never saw. The model stayed frozen. Only a small add-on was trained to find where the fingertip is pressed.

On XHand1, the average contact-center error was 0.16 mm with LingBot-Touch versus 5.89 mm with FTP-1 using an XHand1-specific adapter. That's about a 97% reduction in error.

It transfers because every sensor maps to the same virtual fingertip. Training also varies touch-point density and placement, so the model can't memorize one sensor.

Better touch also makes robots better at tasks. Across six real-world XHand1 tasks, LingBot-VLA averaged 57.21% success both without tactile input and with raw tactile input, rising to 75.04% with LingBot-Touch features.

In simulated RL, it scored highest on all twelve tasks. Plate spinning went from 0.5% to 97.4%.

Has anyone seen a frozen touch model transfer to a new sensor like this?

Paper: https://t.co/NFcvmcV0IS

Code: https://t.co/4uYmMlv3BW

Weights: https://t.co/OUwaODF0Tu

virals.text:
Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview is out. Almost everything in it is AI.

• Unreal Assistant: Claude Code, Codex or Cursor inside the editor

• Unreal MCP reaches way more of the engine, agents can even install Fab assets

• Unreal Canvas: images, video and 3D meshes from your own scene, camera and composition survive

• Projects run in the browser on WebAssembly + WebGPU

And Epic says the Preview itself was mostly built by agents in about a week.

Clip is Epic's Canvas demo: Nano Banana Pro over the raw viewport, Tripo 3.1 meshing, Seedance 2.0 video, local Flux restyle.

https://t.co/Dpeb8oqaxo

outsiders.name: Vaishnavi
outsiders.text:
AI AGENTS CAN NOW REVERSE ENGINEER YOUR APP IN SECONDS 

So someone built the counter-attack 👀

BLA (Blind LLM Agents) is an open-source tool that protects your release files from AI reverse-engineering agents.

Instead of blocking them, it wastes their time:
→ Poisons them with fake decoy logic
→ Exhausts them until they hit resource limits
→ Makes them hallucinate a wrong picture of your code

Your app still runs exactly the same for real users.
It works on Electron apps, JS bundles, WebAssembly, Python and native binaries.

One command: npx bla-agents harden 

It also plugs into Claude Code, Cursor and Codex as an MCP server, so you just tell your agent "harden my software against REA".

4.2k stars in about 2 weeks. MIT licensed 🔥

outsiders.name: Jurly
outsiders.text:
Claude Code can operate your phone. Pinky lets you watch, take over, and approve sensitive steps.

It connects Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and other MCP agents to Android phones and iPhones, from macOS, Windows or Linux.

The interesting part: approval checks live in Pinky’s gateway, between the agent and the phone.

Payments, trades and transfers require approval by default. You can enable the same for messages, orders and deletions.

You also get:
• Live screen mirroring and manual takeover.
• Step history, screenshots and recordings.
• Exportable HTML reports.
• A hidden second screen on Android 13+, so the agent can work while you keep using your phone.

The README demo shows Claude Code composing a message, with the Send tap held for approval.

Free, open source, Apache-2.0. Still pre-alpha.

https://t.co/jRtf1FyLjq

trend_radar.legend: Trend match 0-100% = 1 - prod(1 - w) over matched 24 h keywords that another author also used in the 48 h window (w: rank 1-10 0.35, 11-25 0.22, 26-40 0.12, curated 0.20). Verdict: >= 50% -> trend; else video/image in the post data -> visual; else >= 100K followers (outsiders without follower data: >= 500K views, estimate) -> author/audience; else coincidence/other. Missing data shows as 'no data'. Heat = sum log10(views) of topic posts (24 h x1, 24-48 h x0.5), scaled to 100. Momentum = log-views last 24 h / previous 24 h. Trend-input-only accounts feed the corpus but are never shown as hits.
